summaries.example: Imagine two sentences: “A robin is a bird” and “A robin is a bicycle.” In a simple logic, the first sentence gets the value True and the second gets False. The sentence works like a label pointing to one of these two values. Other logics may add a value for “not settled” or for information that says both True and False.
summaries.summary: A truth value is what a logical system assigns to a sentence. In classical logic, there are two: the True and the False. Gottlob Frege made this idea central to the study of language and logic. He proposed that a complete sentence can be treated somewhat like a name whose referent is the True or the False. Predicates and connecting words can then work like functions: they take objects or truth values as inputs and produce sentences or new truth values. This helps explain how the parts of a sentence contribute to the whole. The idea also raises a philosophical question. Is truth mainly a property, as when we say “that sentence is true,” or can truth be treated as an abstract object? The entry presents both approaches without settling the dispute. It also explains that not every logical system has only two values. Many-valued systems may represent uncertainty, gaps in information, or conflicting information. In these systems, a special set of “designated” values helps determine which sentences count as acceptable in an argument. Thus, truth values are both philosophical ideas about what sentences refer to and practical tools for studying reasoning.
key_ideas: In one familiar system, sentences have two values: True and False.
The philosopher Gottlob Frege treated sentences as referring to special objects called the True and the False.
Words such as “not” and “and” can be understood as rules that work on truth values.
Some logical systems use more than two values, such as “neither true nor false” or “both true and false.”
Philosophers disagree about whether truth should be understood as a property of a sentence, an object, or something analyzed in another way.
summaries.why_it_matters: Truth values help people and computers describe how sentences behave in arguments. They make it possible to test whether a conclusion follows from premises. More flexible systems can also represent situations in which information is missing, unclear, or inconsistent instead of forcing every case into simply True or False.

important_terms.definition: A label used in logic for the result a sentence receives, such as True or False.
A way of checking whether a sentence or argument receives an accepted value in a logical system.
A complete phrase that says something and can be judged true or false, such as “Snow is cold.”
A rule that combines truth values to give a truth value for a larger sentence. For example, “not” changes True to False in classical logic.

questions_to_think_about: Could a sentence be neither true nor false? When might that happen?
Does calling a sentence “true” add information, or does it simply repeat what the sentence says?
If two sentences have the same truth value, must they mean the same thing?
Why might a computer need a value for information that is incomplete or conflicting?

summaries.example: Suppose a database receives two reports about proposition P: one says “The sensor is working,” and another says “The sensor is not working.” A classical system must assign P either True or False, but a four-valued system can represent four information states: evidence for P only, evidence against P only, no evidence either way, or evidence for both. The extra values need not mean that truth itself comes in numerical degrees; they can instead record how information bears on P.
summaries.summary: The entry studies truth values as tools in semantics and as candidates for a distinctive kind of abstract object. Frege’s influential proposal begins with a functional analysis of language. Proper names refer to objects, functional expressions refer to functions, and a completed sentence is treated as a name whose referent is either the True or the False. Predicates and connectives can therefore be modeled as functions whose outputs are truth values. This gives a systematic account of compositionality and of the preservation of truth in valid inference. It also motivates the slingshot argument, a family of arguments claiming that sentences connected through reference-preserving steps end up sharing only their truth value as a common designation. The entry notes that this conclusion has been disputed. A separate distinction concerns the category of truth. In ordinary grammar, “true” looks like a predicate of sentences or propositions. Fregean semantics instead treats the True and the False as objects, while other approaches analyze truth as a property or in another way. Treating truth values as abstract objects raises questions about their identity and ontology. The discussion then turns to logical systems. A valuation system specifies values, connective-functions, and designated values; entailment is defined by preserving designatedness from premises to conclusions. Classical logic uses two values, but many-valued systems may include intermediate, incomplete, or conflicting statuses. The entry emphasizes that these added values can be interpreted in different ways and that their philosophical meaning is contested. key_ideas: Frege’s analysis treats sentences as complete expressions that refer to truth values, while predicates and connectives can be analyzed as functions.
This framework supports compositionality and helps explain why logical connectives can be represented by truth-value functions.
Truth as a property and truth as an object are different philosophical categories; the entry explains motivations for each rather than declaring one the winner.
A valuation system can use two values or many values. Its designated values determine which valuations count for tautology and entailment.

Many-valued systems do not automatically show that there are many logical values in the deepest philosophical sense. Suszko’s thesis argues that many algebraic values can still support a two-way distinction between designated and undesignated.
Structured and generalized values, including four-valued systems, can represent incomplete or conflicting information.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory of truth values connects abstract questions about truth with concrete methods for evaluating arguments, building logical systems, and representing information. It clarifies why classical logic works so uniformly while also showing how alternative systems can handle gaps, contradictions, vagueness, or different kinds of information. The disagreements matter because changing the interpretation of a value can change what counts as a valid inference.

important_terms.definition: An abstract semantic value assigned to a sentence; in classical logic the values are commonly the True and the False.
A function or rule that maps the values of component sentences to the value of a compound sentence.
The principle that the meaning or value of a complex expression is fixed by the meanings or values of its parts and their arrangement.
A semantic system consisting of a set of values, a chosen set of designated values, and functions interpreting logical connectives.
A value counted as acceptable for purposes such as defining tautologies or preserving consequence.
The relation between premises and a conclusion defined by preservation of designated values.
A view that truth is an attribute of a sentence, proposition, belief, or another truth-bearer.
A view associated with Frege in which the True and the False are abstract objects referred to by sentences.

questions_to_think_about: If “It is true that P” has the same content as P, why might a theory still treat the True as an object?
Does a three-valued system represent a third kind of truth, or merely an additional semantic status?
Why does the choice of designated values matter for logical consequence?
Can a truth-functional system adequately represent vague predicates, or might vagueness require a different kind of semantics?
What does the slingshot-style reasoning try to show about what true sentences refer to, and what assumptions might a critic challenge?

summaries.example: A school app stores a statement about a quiz answer: “Maya chose option B.” If the answer record is clear, the statement might receive True or False. But if the record is missing, a three-valued system might use a third status such as “undetermined.” If two records disagree, a four-valued system can keep both pieces of information instead of erasing one. These extra statuses help describe the information without pretending that every case fits ordinary two-valued logic.
summaries.summary: Truth values are the semantic statuses used by logical systems to evaluate sentences. In classical logic, a sentence is assigned one of two values, True or False. The entry explains the influential account associated with Gottlob Frege. Frege separates names, which refer to objects, from functional expressions, which need arguments. He then treats complete sentences as a special kind of name referring to the True or the False. A predicate applied to a name produces a sentence, and a connective such as “not” or “and” can be represented as a function that operates on truth values. This approach helps make language analysis systematic: the value of a complex sentence depends on the values of its components and the way they are joined. It also leads to the idea that logic studies the relations and rules governing logical values. The entry contrasts two ways of thinking about truth. On one view, truth is a property possessed by sentences, propositions, or beliefs. On another, the True and the False are abstract objects to which sentences refer. The slingshot argument supports the second picture by using a sequence of reference-preserving transformations, although the argument and its assumptions have been debated. The entry also describes valuation systems. These specify possible values, connective rules, and designated values. A conclusion is entailed when designatedness is preserved from the premises. Classical logic uses two values, while many-valued logics may use a third status for a gap or indeterminacy, or values that represent both supporting and opposing information. The source stresses that extra values can be interpreted in different ways; they need not all be understood as degrees of truth. key_ideas: Frege’s theory gives sentences a special role: they can be treated as names whose references are truth values.
Predicates and connectives can be understood as functions, making it possible to calculate the value of a larger sentence from its parts.
Philosophers distinguish the familiar idea of truth as a property from the less familiar idea of truth as an object.
Classical logic has two values, but many-valued logics introduce additional values or statuses for different purposes.
Designated values are especially important because they determine how tautologies and logical consequence are defined.
The entry presents disagreements about slingshot arguments, truth-bearers, vagueness, and whether many-valued systems really contain many logical values.
summaries.why_it_matters: Learning about truth values shows how a simple idea—classifying sentences—supports both philosophical analysis and formal reasoning. It helps explain truth tables, logical consequence, and computer systems that manage incomplete or conflicting data. It also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a familiar word such as “true” can hide several different questions about language, objects, meaning, and information.

important_terms.definition: The result assigned to a sentence by a logical system, often True or False.
A sentence part that acts like a rule, taking an input and producing an output; logical connectives can work this way.
The idea that a complex expression gets its meaning or logical value from its parts and how they are combined.
A formal setup that lists its possible values, its accepted or designated values, and the rules for connectives.
A value treated as acceptable when deciding whether a sentence is a logical law or whether an argument preserves correctness.
A logical relation in which acceptable values of the premises guarantee an acceptable value for the conclusion.
A view in which being true is something a sentence, belief, or proposition has.
A view in which the True and the False are treated as abstract things that sentences can refer to.

questions_to_think_about: If two sentences are both true, are they thereby alike in meaning?
What is gained by treating a sentence as referring to the True or the False?
Should “undetermined” count as a truth value, or is it a lack of information?
How could a logical system represent a report that is supported and contradicted at the same time?
Why might different choices of designated values produce different notions of valid reasoning?
